model:gemini|title:ai agents now control.content_excerpt: Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors. According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act. Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people. The model reads, edits and runs things under the person's rules, and it keeps its plan in mem , in Gno, on disk. Each step of a task is a frame: when the step is done and popped, its work leaves what the model is sent and its result stays, the way a function's locals go when it returns. A new session starts from what is still open. It runs. Built from this tree, it has answered prompts, used tools, asked permission, planned and finished a task in mem , and popped frames against a real model (Qwen 3.8 27B on llama.cpp). tools/dev/remote-ci.sh builds, vets and tests every package from a clean copy. In a session, Claude Code's commands work as there: /help , /clear , /restart (gnosh starts again in the same session, the newer one once a new build is installed, which the session says), /background (the session goes on without the terminal, as a run of its own on the prompt given), /fork (a copy of the conversation works on the prompt in the background while this session goes on), /subtask (as /fork , and what the copy answers comes back to this conversation when it is done), /compact , /resume (by number, id, name, or words from a session's name or first prompt), /branch , /rewind (the conversation, the files Write and Edit changed, or both, the files as they were when the prompt went out, whatever changed them since; what a file holds is kept before it is put back, and the copies of your 100 most recent prompts are kept; or a summary of what followed a prompt, going back to before it, or of what came before it), /model , /effort , /config , /plan , /permissions , /add-dir , /cd (the session moves to another folder and goes on there, with that folder's settings, instructions and skills; Cd rules say where it may go), /status , /context , /btw (a side question, also while the model works; nothing of it is kept), /recap , /color (this session's prompt mark in a colour of its own, kept with the session), /keybindings (Claude Code's keybindings.json: a key bound to an action, null to take one away, command: to run one), /cost , /tasks , /diff , /export , /copy , /init , /memory , /agents , /mcp (with reconnect, enable and disable), /skills , /reload-skills , /hooks , /statusline , /debug (debug logging on, and the model finds out from gnosh's log what went wrong) and /doctor , with gnosh's own /mem , /goal , /loop and

story|title:ai driven terraform move fas.content_excerpt: Having AI write IaC is no longer unusual. It can add a module, change a few resources, and draft policy much faster than a person. That speed brings a different problem. A change can pull in unrelated resources. Terraform that is perfectly valid can still delete or replace resources, or loosen permissions. Those issues are not always obvious in code review. As the volume grows, reviewing every line by hand stops scaling. Handing the review to another AI adds another opinion, not another guarantee. The real question is this: how can AI keep writing and iterating while its mistakes are caught consistently and kept out of production? I reduce it to three steps: define what AI may change, verify the result with scripts and policy, then leave production writes to human approval and CI/CD. Within that scope, AI can generate code, make small commits, and revise its work from concrete errors. Scripts check formatting, syntax, change scope, and plan risk. Policy checks infrastructure rules. Repository changes and production writes follow separate paths. AI may change code on a controlled branch. A person approves merges, live policy changes, and production changes; CI/CD performs the approved operation. AI does not need to be limited to a few lines, but every task needs a clear scope. If the task is to adjust one database connection, it should not also change unrelated resources or refactor a module. These checks do not require a model to understand the business context, and their result should not depend on how the model interprets them. Local checks give AI a quick feedback loop. CI provides the final gate. Reusing the same scripts and rules in both places avoids changes that pass locally and fail under a different standard after submission. Formatting and syntax only cover the code layer. Policy should manage the rules that govern infrastructure security and platform standards. If the current environment supports tfpolicy , existing rules can move over gradually. The toolset can converge over time, but rule migration still needs semantic equivalence. Merge duplicate rules and keep checks that tfpolicy does not yet cover. tfpolicy can tell whether a resource follows platform rules. It does not necessarily know what the original ticket intended to change. For example, a ticket may only update a Storage Account tag while the Plan also replaces a database. story|title:linux of ai score and prove.content_excerpt: Linux of AI is a free, open-source ecosystem for building portable, governed, measurable, and replaceable AI infrastructure. It connects tools for agent orchestration, private deployment, model switching, policy, ontology, audit logs, and AI cost measurement to help reduce vendor lock-in. Build AI systems that are inspectable, governed, measurable, replaceable, and not trapped inside a single vendor. Overview • Mission • The Problem • Projects • Screenshots • Architecture • Principles • Get Started Linux of AI makes it cheap and provable to leave any AI vendor. Vendors are where things run ; your Git repository is where things are defined . Every package is Beta, Apache-2.0, runs offline by default, and supports Python 3.11 to 3.13. ai-suite exit-report scores how hard it would be to leave a vendor on twelve vectors, each from 0 (most portable) to 100 (most locked, or no evidence): policies · prompts · embeddings · fine-tunes · memory · audit history · cost history · tool connectors · identities · ontology · contract terms · model providers Every row states which checks the scanner re-ran itself and which claims stay operator-attested. The suite never runs a model. Restores are verified against deterministic offline fake profiles, not real vendor restores, and contract terms are always attested. See the exit report documentation . New to Linux of AI? Start with the Start Here guide to choose the right tool for your problem. You can also inspect the Linux of AI Vendor Exit Demo to see the ecosystem pattern in one deterministic, offline-first example. The three-profile restore demo separately verifies content, behavior, and re-export gates against provider-shaped offline fakes (Azure-, AWS-, and Ollama-shaped), including a chained migration through all three profiles. It is not a real vendor restore. It uses deterministic fixture data, requires only the Python standard library, and makes no external API calls. See the Quickstart Kit guide for the generated file map, replacement workflow, and limitations. The Linux of AI Vendor Exit Demo shows how the ecosystem can help a team evaluate replacing an expensive or locked-in AI model using portable ontology, policy, benchmarking, audit evidence, and cost/outcome measurement. story|title:muxlio durable workflow orch.content_excerpt: Muxlio is a durable workflow coordinator for multi-step work across AI agents and shell tools. Your assistant authors an immutable plan; the coordinator runs it as a durable run you can follow in the bundled UI or through MCP after setup. Use Muxlio when work needs dependent steps, verification, retries, or hand-offs—not for one-off answers in the client. You or your assistant authors a workflow ; Muxlio compiles it to an immutable plan and executes a run on the coordinator . Steps run on workers through adapters (agent CLIs, remote A2A, command , and others). Setup ports and MCP clients: Setup defaults . Architecture: overview and how it works . I use this recipe to develop Muxlio itself. The workflow handles one feature at a time and runs the repository’s build and tests before creating a local commit. Describe the steps and checks you want. Your assistant authors and validates a workflow, then starts a run with your inputs. Check the plan before starting the run. An agent implements the feature. A review step inspects and improves the change. Build and test commands run. If a check fails, an agent gets the failure report, fixes it, and the checks run again. After checks pass, the recipe creates a local commit and moves to the next feature. Inspect the diff, review notes, test output, and run history. You decide whether to push. I run Muxlio on a Mac mini and start workflows through my assistant. In the morning, I check the commits and reports. If a run stopped, I read the error and decide what to do next. The chat can be closed while it runs. You choose where it runs: your workstation, another computer, or a server. Keep the execution machine running and use the UI or your assistant to check progress. Use Homebrew on macOS or Linux. It installs the CLI, adapters, UI, and MCP server without a manual checkout. init prepares workspace configuration, credentials, and agent instructions; service start runs the coordinator and worker. Default ports and MCP client rules match Start Muxlio → Setup defaults . Verify stdio MCP with the MCP guide when appropriate, then ask your assistant to build a workflow for your task, validate it, and show you the plan before running it. You do not need Muxlio's source repository to use the installed service. The worker needs the files and tools your workflow uses. story|title:why is every agent orchestra.content_excerpt: Every week there is a new AI agent orchestrator on my timeline, and every week it is the exact same app . Conductor, Orca, Jean, Intent, Opensession, whatever launched on Hacker News this morning. Blur out the logos on the landing pages and you genuinely cannot tell them apart. The recipe is always identical. Wrap Claude Code or Codex. Spin up a git worktree per task. Put them in a dark-mode sidebar. Bolt on a diff viewer, an embedded terminal, maybe a Kanban board if you're feeling spicy. Call it an Agent Development Environment and ship it. I honestly don't get it. We are at one of those rare moments where we have a brand-new primitive and nobody actually knows what the right UX for it is yet. On top of that, building software has never been cheaper or faster. You would think people would be taking wild swings right now—making weird, broken, interesting experiments just to see what sticks. Instead, the entire industry immediately settled on the most boring idea possible and started cloning it over and over. Part of it is probably that low friction kills originality . When you can throw together a desktop app in a weekend, you don't sit around thinking deeply about the problem for a month. You just build the very first obvious thing that pops into your head. And because half of these apps are being built using the exact same coding agents they wrap, the tools are basically reproducing themselves. Ask an LLM to build a multi-agent desktop app and it is going to hand you Electron or Tauri, xterm.js, Monaco, and git worktree every single time. The bigger issue is that nobody is questioning the premise . Everyone just looked at a single-player IDE, multiplied the tabs by five, and called it a day. The entire UX assumes your job is to sit there and babysit streaming terminals. Watch five agents type, click approve, squint at five different diffs, repeat. Spawning five agents in parallel is the easy part. You can do that with a ten-line shell script and tmux . The actual bottleneck is reviewing, verifying, and integrating five concurrent streams of code without losing your mind. Putting five terminals next to each other doesn't solve that. It just turns you into a stressed-out air traffic controller. And git worktree is a pretty lazy abstraction for this anyway. It isolates your files, sure, but the second you're working on anything more complicated than a static site, five parallel worktrees are all fighting over the same local ports and the same database. story|ver:2.5|title:taking trainium3 to.content_excerpt: Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine ( trn3.48xlarge , 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work. With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos? I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result. I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API. For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines. The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened: Each shot has a name and a prompt , and can have a seed , to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next: Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames ( to ), and the shots after it start from its last frames ( from ).
